tip: Korean normally leaves the question word in place: 뭐 (mwo = what) sits right where the answer will – 뭐 할 거예요? (mwo hal geoyeyo). The reply slots into the same spot.
저녁 (jeonyeok) means the evening AND the meal you eat then – here 저녁에 (jeonyeoge) = for dinner. One word covers both; context decides.
Clock hours use native Korean numbers: 여덟 시 (yeodeol si = eight o'clock), never Sino 팔 (pal). Minutes switch back to Sino numbers.
살 거예요 (sal geoyeyo) is ambiguous: 사다 (sada = buy) and 살다 (salda = live) both shorten to 살. Only context – here 옷을 (oseul = clothes) – says it's 'buy'.
The everyday way to negate a future is 안 before the verb: 안 할 거예요 (an hal geoyeyo = won't do).
산에 가다 (sane gada) = go hiking – Koreans say 'go to the mountain'.
놀다 (nolda) is 'play' with no kid connotation – adults use it too: 친구랑 놀 거예요 (chingurang nol geoyeyo) = I'll hang out with a friend.
Many English nouns become Korean verbs with 하다 (hada = do): 쇼핑할 거예요 (syopinghal geoyeyo) = will 'do shopping'. Loanwords plug straight in.
푹 (puk) is the go-to intensifier for rest and sleep: 푹 쉴 거예요 (puk swil geoyeyo) = rest up properly; 푹 자요 (puk jayo) = sleep soundly.
내년에 (naenyeone = next year) keeps its 에 (e), but 오늘, 내일, 어제 (oneul, naeil, eoje = today, tomorrow, yesterday) drop it – the everyday trio goes bare.
(으)로 marks the means: 기차로 (gicharo = by train). There's no word for 'by' – the ending glued onto the noun does the job.
Durations normally need no word for 'for' – the bare time phrase is enough: 삼 일 있을 거예요 (sam il isseul geoyeyo) = we'll stay three days.
짐을 싸다 (jimeul ssada) = pack your bags – same 싸다 as the one meaning 'cheap', context decides.
'With' is 랑 (rang) after vowels but 이랑 (irang) after consonants: 부모님이랑 (bumonimirang = with my parents). Casual speech only.
휴가 (hyuga) = your days off; 여행 (yeohaeng) = the trip you take on them.
'There will be' is just 있다 (itda = exist): 회의가 있을 거예요 (hoeiga isseul geoyeyo) = a meeting will exist. No word for 'there'.
새 (sae = new) only works in front of a noun: 새 프로젝트 (sae peurojekteu). To say something IS new you need the verb form 새로워요 (saerowoyo).
바쁘다 (bappeuda = busy) turns straight into 바쁠 거예요 (bappeul geoyeyo = will be busy) – adjectives take the future like verbs, no 'be' needed.
님 (nim) honors titles, and the verb takes 시: 사장님이 오실 거예요 (sajangnimi osil geoyeyo).
(으)ㄹ 거예요 also predicts: 비가 올 거예요 (biga ol geoyeyo = it'll rain).
Snow usually comes rather than falls in Korean: 눈이 올 거예요 (nuni ol geoyeyo = snow will come). Rain uses 오다 (oda = come) too.
You won't find 추울 (chuul) in the dictionary – it's 춥다 (chupda = cold): the ㅂ (b) turns to 우 (u) before a vowel ending, giving 추울 거예요 (chuul geoyeyo).
Korean flips 'need': the thing needed is the subject – 우산이 필요할 거예요 (usani piryohal geoyeyo) = 'an umbrella will be necessary', not 'you'll need'.
약속 (yaksok) = both 'promise' and 'plans with someone' – 약속이 있어요 (yaksogi isseoyo) = I have plans.
돈을 모으다 (doneul moeuda) = save money – literally 'gather' it.
부터 (buteo = from, starting) glues onto time words: 내일부터 (naeilbuteo = from tomorrow). English puts 'from' before; Korean attaches it after.
친구를 사귀다 (chingureul sagwida) = make friends – 만들다 (mandeulda = make) normally isn't used for people.
동생 (dongsaeng) = any younger sibling, brother or sister – it doesn't mark gender. Add 여 (yeo) or 남 (nam) in front only if gender matters.
You call TO someone: 할머니한테 전화할 거예요 (halmeonihante jeonhwahal geoyeyo) – 한테 (hante = to) marks the person, not the object marker 를 (reul).
언니 (eonni = older sister) is what FEMALE speakers say – a man calls his older sister 누나 (nuna). The speaker's gender picks the word.
